tip: In the simple past, 'querer' marks a completed act of wanting, so 'a gente quis ajudar' can also suggest we tried to help.
'Estava dormindo' is the ongoing background in the past, and 'tocou' is the one-time event that interrupts it.
'Fazer de conta' means 'to pretend.' 'Faz de conta que é da casa' is a warm invitation to feel comfortable.
'Perguntou se' means asked whether: 'se' introduces an indirect question, reporting it rather than quoting it.
'Porque', one word with no accent, means 'because': 'abri a janela porque' = I opened the window because.
'Perder' covers both to lose and to miss something scheduled: 'perdemos o voo' = we missed the flight.
'Que' plus a noun makes what a, so 'que pena' means what a shame, the same shape as 'que sorte' or 'que legal'.
'Soube' is the past of 'saber' and means found out or realized, not 'knew': 'a gente soube na hora'.
Name the means of transport with 'de': 'veio de ônibus' = came by bus, like 'de carro' = by car.
Portuguese makes a trip rather than takes one: 'fez uma viagem' means took a trip, using 'fazer' instead of 'tomar'.
'Tomar banho' = to take a shower. 'Tomar' (to take) is the usual verb for showers and drinks: 'tomava banho'.
'Pegar leve' means to go easy on someone; here 'pega leve' = go easy on him. The opposite is 'pegar pesado' (to be harsh or to overdo it).
'Almoçava' is the habitual past (I used to have lunch), while 'almocei' is today's one-time event: habit vs single action.
'Torcer para' means to root for or cheer for a team, so 'torceu para' = cheered for. Flamengo is Brazil's most popular soccer team.
'Feijoada' is Brazil's national dish – a rich black bean stew with pork, traditionally served on Wednesdays and Saturdays.
'Curtir' is informal Brazilian for enjoy or have fun, so 'curtiu a praia' means enjoyed the beach.
'A tempo' means in time, while 'no prazo' means by the deadline, so 'terminou a tempo' means he finished in time.
For this -ir verb the 'nós' form is the same in present and past, so 'dividimos' can mean we split or we are splitting.
Portuguese makes friendship rather than becomes friends, so 'fez amizade com' means became friends with.
'Experimentar' looks like experiment but usually means to try, especially food, so 'experimentaram o açaí' means did you try the açaí.
Don't confuse 'viemos' (we came) with 'vimos' (we saw); they are different verbs that sound close.
'Combinar de' plus an infinitive means to arrange or agree to, so 'combinou de se encontrar' means arranged to meet.
In the simple past 'saber' shifts to found out, so 'soube da notícia' means I found out the news, not I already knew it.
'Dar uma olhada' is literally to give a look and means to take a look, so 'deram uma olhada' means did you take a look.
'Voltamos' is both present and past for this verb; here 'ontem' is what tells you it means we came back yesterday.
'A gente' means we but takes the singular verb form used with 'ele' or 'ela': 'a gente viajou', not 'viajamos'.
'Poder' in the past: 'a gente pôde'. The accent tells them apart: 'pôde' (was able) vs 'pode' (can, present).
'Não deu' is extremely common Brazilian Portuguese for 'it didn't work out' or 'it wasn't possible.' Short for 'não deu certo.'
Here 'fui' comes from 'ser' (to be), not 'ir' (to go). 'Eu fui o primeiro' = I was the first. Context clarifies.
'Sabia' is the ongoing 'knew' (I knew how to swim); 'soube' would mean 'found out' at one moment.
